B1.1.1.q: A retail chain links the networks in its shops across the country so stock data is shared. Which network type is this?
B1.1.1.why: A WAN links networks over a large geographical area.

B1.1.2.q: A company gives trusted suppliers controlled access to part of its private network to check orders. What is this?
B1.1.2.why: An intranet is for staff only; an extranet extends limited access to approved outsiders.

B1.1.3.q: An office connects Wi-Fi access points to its wired Ethernet backbone. What extra security issue does the wireless part add?
options: Signals can be picked up outside the building
It removes the need for a firewall
B1.1.3.why: Integrating wireless widens the attack surface, because radio leaks beyond physical walls.

B1.1.4.q: A security consultant redraws a network diagram to show a firewall added between the router and the switch. What kind of diagram is this?
B1.1.4.why: Schematic diagrams show network layout, sometimes with ports or addresses.

B1.1.5.q: A business needs its network to keep running if one link fails, and to grow as it opens new sites. Which features are these?
B1.1.5.why: Network requirements include surviving failures and allowing growth. Many are linked to security.

B1.2.q: In a network, every device connects to a central switch. If the switch fails, what happens?
options: The whole network stops (single point of failure)
Nothing, as it is fully meshed
B1.2.why: In a star topology, the central device is a single point of failure.

B1.3.q: Every PC in a small office shares files directly with the others, with no central server managing security. What is the security weakness of this architecture?
options: Peer-to-peer has no central control of security
Data can't be shared at all
B1.3.why: Client/server gives central control; peer-to-peer leaves security up to each machine.

B1.4.1.q: A security team runs a suspicious file inside an isolated virtual machine so it can't harm the real system. Which trend is this?
B1.4.1.why: Virtualisation runs isolated VMs on one physical host.

B1.4.2.q: A company's cloud storage bucket is left publicly readable by default settings, exposing customer files. Which trend's security issue is this?
B1.4.2.why: Cloud risks include misconfiguration, hijacked accounts and less control over data.

B1.4.3a.q: Staff read company email on their own phones, which have no passcode and run unvetted apps. Which trend creates this risk?
B1.4.3a.why: BYOD mixes personal and company data on devices the organisation doesn't control.

B1.4.3b.q: A home worker connects to company systems over unsecured home Wi-Fi, next to an insecure smart camera. What should the company require?
B1.4.3b.why: Remote working and IoT bring risks such as insecure home networks. A VPN encrypts the connection.

B2.1.1.q: Which group lists only end-user devices?
B2.1.1.why: End-user devices are the ones people use directly, both mobile and fixed.

B2.1.2.q: Which device joins a company's LAN to the internet and directs packets between the two networks?
B2.1.2.why: Connectivity devices direct traffic. A router joins networks; a switch connects devices within a LAN.

B2.1.3.q: A bank links two buildings with a medium that is fast, works over long distances and is very hard to tap. Which medium is this?
B2.1.3.why: Connection media carry the data. Fibre is fast, long-range and hard to intercept.

B2.2.q: An employee finds a USB stick in the car park and plugs it into a work PC to see whose it is. What is the main risk?
options: The PC running out of storage
B2.2.why: External media can carry malware or be lost with data on them.

B2.3.q: An administrator uses a packet sniffer to watch traffic for suspicious activity. Which network component is this?
B2.3.why: Software components include OSs, monitoring tools and applications running on the network.

B3.1.1.q: When a file is sent across a network, which protocol suite splits it into packets and addresses them to the destination?
B3.1.1.why: TCP splits data into packets and IP addresses and routes them.

B3.1.4.q: Ten devices in a home all reach the internet using one public IP address. What makes this possible?
B3.1.4.why: NAT maps private internal addresses to one public address, which also hides internal devices.

B3.2.q: A hotel puts guest Wi-Fi on a separate segment from its booking and payment systems. What is the security benefit?
options: An attacker on guest Wi-Fi can't easily reach staff systems
It removes the need for passwords
B3.2.why: Segmentation controls access and limits how far an attacker can spread.

B3.3.q: Which network configuration device should be set to block all inbound traffic except on the ports the business needs?
B3.3.why: Firewalls filter traffic using rules; routers direct packets.

B3.4.1.q: A user types www.example.com, and the computer needs the matching IP address. Which service provides it?
B3.4.1.why: DNS turns domain names into IP addresses. Poisoned DNS can redirect users to fake sites.

B3.4.4.q: A visitor's laptop joins the office Wi-Fi and is given an IP address and gateway automatically. Which service did this?
B3.4.4.why: DHCP automatically gives devices an IP address and network settings.

B3.5.1.q: Staff save shared documents to one central server and send print jobs to a queue that manages the office printers. Which services are these?
B3.5.1.why: File and print services provide shared storage and printing across a network.

B3.5.2.q: A company's email is sent using SMTP with no encryption added. What is the risk?
options: Messages could be read if intercepted
B3.5.2.why: Some web, mail and communication services have no built-in encryption, so TLS or HTTPS must be added.
